summary: Defines two link relation types, create-form and edit-form, that let a web resource point to an input form for creating or editing data. It builds on the web linking framework of RFC 5988. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Name tags for links on the web: one says here is the form to make a new thing, and the other says here is the form to change it.

subtitle: Two standard link names for web forms that create or edit resources.

tldr.problem: Web servers need a standard way to tell clients where to find a form for creating a new resource or editing an existing one. Without standards, every API invents its own naming convention.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6861 defines two link relation types: `create-form` points to a form for adding a new member to a collection, and `edit-form` points to a form for updating a resource. Both are registered with IANA and use the web linking framework from RFC 5988.
tldr.outcome: Web clients can now discover and use forms for creating and editing data, and servers have a standard way to advertise them. The relations are generic and can be used with multiple media types.

facts.label: Form media types
facts.value: Generic, works with any media type

today: RFC 6861 is an informational document that has not been obsoleted. The create-form and edit-form link relations are registered with IANA and are standard for web applications that use forms.

sections.title: Web Linking and Link Relations
sections.content:
RFC 5988 standardized the concept of link relations, which describe the relationship between resources on the web. A link relation tells a client what a linked resource represents. For example, a rel="alternate" link means the target is an alternate version of the current resource; rel="next" means the next item in a sequence.

This RFC defines two new link relation types for a common use case: forms. When a web resource wants to let clients know where to find a form for creating or editing data, it can use the standard `create-form` or `edit-form` relation to advertise the form's location. Without a standard, every API uses different conventions, making it hard for generic clients to find forms automatically.
sections.eli5: Web links have names describing what they point to. This document adds two new standard names: one for a form that creates a new thing, and one for a form that edits something.

sections.title: The Two Link Relations
sections.content:
The create-form link relation indicates a resource that is a form for adding a new member to a collection. When a client follows a create-form link, it receives a form that it can fill out and submit to create a new entry.

The edit-form link relation indicates a resource that is a form for updating an existing resource. A client can use this form to modify the current resource.

A server can advertise these links in two ways. In HTML, using the <a> tag with rel="create-form" or rel="edit-form". Alternatively, in a Link HTTP header:

Link: </forms/entry>; rel="create-form"; title="Add New Entry"

The links can include optional attributes like title to describe the form to users.
sections.eli5: Create-form points to a form for making a new entry. Edit-form points to a form for changing an existing one. Servers list these links like directions.

sections.title: How to Use These Relations
sections.content:
When a client gets a form through a create-form or edit-form link, the form representation itself may specify where to submit and how.

For create-form: If the form includes a submission URI, that URI MUST be used. Otherwise, the client SHOULD use the URI of the current resource. If the form specifies an HTTP method, that method MUST be used. Otherwise, clients SHOULD use POST.

For edit-form: If the form includes a submission URI, that URI MUST be used. Otherwise, the client SHOULD use the URI of the current resource. If the form specifies an HTTP method, that method MUST be used. Otherwise, clients SHOULD use PUT.

These relations are intentionally generic and can be used with multiple media types and in a wide variety of use cases. A server can even return a create-form link in an error response, for example when the client submits data in an unsupported format.
sections.eli5: The form tells you where to send it and what HTTP command to use. If it doesn't, use POST for creating and PUT for editing. It works with any kind of web data.

sections.title: Registration and Status
sections.content:
RFC 6861 registers both link relation types with IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) according to the procedures in RFC 5988. This ensures the names are officially recognized and documented.

Both relations are generic and can be used in any context where a form is needed for creating or editing. Automated agents and clients should be aware that following these links might take them to resources in different administrative domains (different websites or authorities), and they should apply appropriate security measures.

RFC 6861 is informational and has not been obsoleted. The link relations are now standards for web linking.
sections.eli5: These link names are officially registered, so everyone uses the same standard names. Be careful if a link takes you to a different website.
